body:
in History, Language Lessons |   	October 22nd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	


Latin is a lan­guage
As dead as dead can be; 
It killed the Romans long ago, 
And now it’s killing me.

That famed dit­ty isn’t like­ly to res­onate with many mod­ern school chil­dren, but inter­est in ancient Rome remains fair­ly robust. 
We’ve come to accept that those state­ly ruins were once cov­ered in graf­fi­ti.
We can recre­ate their meals from hors d’oeuvres (Boiled Eggs with Pine Nut Sauce) to dessert (Pear Pati­na).
Ther­mae Romae, a pop­u­lar Japan­ese man­ga-cum-fea­ture-film, took us inside Emper­or Hadri­an’s bath­house.
But what did the Romans sound like?
Kirk Dou­glas’ Spar­ta­cus? Or Lau­rence Olivier’s Cras­sus?
The HBO series Rome upheld the tra­di­tion of British accents.
Ani­ma­tor Josh Rud­der of NativLang did a fair amount of dig­ging in ser­vice of find­ing out What Latin Sound­ed Like, above.
(And he seems to have done so with­out the help of Derek Jarman’s NSFW Sebas­tiane, the only fea­ture film to be filmed entire­ly in ser­mo vul­garis or vul­gar Latin.)
Instead, he draws from ancient rhetori­cian Quin­til­ian and Virgil’s poet­ic meter. Scroll back­ward through the Romance lan­guages, and you’ll see Ger­man­ic tribes trad­ing with and fight­ing ancient Roman troops.
The result is not so much a recon­struc­tive pro­nun­ci­a­tion guide as a lin­guis­tic detec­tive sto­ry.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

Ayun Hal­l­i­day is an author, illus­tra­tor, the­ater mak­er and Chief Pri­ma­tol­o­gist in NYC.

title: In 1897, London’s Lampposts Dispensed Hot Coffee, Tea, and “Fluid Beef”
description: Any read­er of Vic­to­ri­an lit­er­a­ture will won­der how much a ha’pen­ny was actu­al­ly worth in those days. For a lit­tle more than a year at
body:
Any read­er of Vic­to­ri­an lit­er­a­ture will won­der how much a ha’pen­ny was actu­al­ly worth in those days. For a lit­tle more than a year at the very end of that peri­od, it could buy you a cup of cof­fee, cocoa, milk, tea, or “flu­id beef” — which would pour out of a lamp­post on the cor­ner. The Plu­to Lamp, as it was brand­ed, made its debut at the Vic­to­ri­an Era Exhi­bi­tion, which was held in 1897 to cel­e­brate the Queen’s Dia­mond Jubilee. Amid such attrac­tions as a 360-degree panora­ma of ancient Rome, Pep­per’s ghost illu­sions, and over 1,200 works of art by the likes of J. M. W. Turn­er, John Con­sta­ble, and 180 spe­cial­ly select­ed female artists, a bev­er­age-dis­pens­ing street­light might seem mun­dane. Yet apart from being a tech­no­log­i­cal mar­vel in its own way, it also pre­saged the tech­nol­o­gy-sat­u­rat­ed streets one day to come.
Not long after the Vic­to­ri­an Era Exhi­bi­tion, Plu­to Lamps appeared in sev­er­al Lon­don loca­tions, includ­ing Exmouth Street in Clerken­well, Leices­ter Square, and Rose­bery Avenue. In addi­tion to the illu­mi­na­tion of their sur­round­ings, and the drinks warmed by the excess heat thus gen­er­at­ed, they in some cas­es offered post­cards and four-to-the-pen­ny cig­a­rettes for sale as well.
How­ev­er much atten­tion the Plu­to Lamps attract­ed as a nov­el­ty, this was still the infan­cy of the mod­ern vend­ing machine, whose defi­cien­cies had yet to be ful­ly worked out. It proved impos­si­ble, at the time, to defeat the enter­pris­ing scoundrels who used round pieces of tin in place of gen­uine cur­ren­cy, and in any case, main­te­nance costs seem to have proven unex­pect­ed­ly high. (To say noth­ing of the prospect of drink­ing out of an enam­el cup on a chain, shared with the entire pub­lic, which sure­ly put off even some Vic­to­ri­ans.)
All of the Plu­to Lamps were decom­mis­sioned before the end of the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry, but they’d done their bit to expand pub­lic ideas of what was pos­si­ble in the urban pub­lic realm. “For over a cen­tu­ry, lamp posts would again do lit­tle more than shine light on to the city streets below,” writes Lukas Neck­er­mann in Smart Cities, Smart Mobil­i­ty. “But by the ear­ly twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, the spir­it of the Plu­to Lamps returned. City infra­struc­ture and street fur­ni­ture would once again become mul­ti-pur­pose, mul­ti-use, entre­pre­neur­ial, and con­nect­ed.” And indeed, though talk of “smart cities” may now sound as dat­ed and unap­peal­ing as that of flu­id beef, lamp­posts have more recent­ly been giv­en such side jobs as vehi­cle charg­ing, envi­ron­men­tal pro­tec­tion, and even crime pre­ven­tion. That last brings back to mind the Clerken­well Plu­to Lamp, equipped as it was with a tele­graph recorder con­nect­ed straight to Scot­land Yard: a device that, had it last­ed longer, might have inspired many a Vic­to­ri­an nov­el­ist.
via Messy­Nessy

title: Sears Sold 75,000 DIY Mail Order Homes Between 1908 and 1939, and Transformed American Life
description: Two of the books that most shaped Amer­i­can cul­ture both hap­pened to bear the nick­name “The Big Book.” While the sec­ond of these, the A.
body:
Two of the books that most shaped Amer­i­can cul­ture both hap­pened to bear the nick­name “The Big Book.” While the sec­ond of these, the A.A. Man­u­al, pub­lished in 1939, changed the coun­try with 12-Step recov­ery groups, the first of these, the Sears Cat­a­log, trans­formed Amer­i­ca with mass con­sump­tion, offer­ing cus­tomers in every part of the coun­try access to mod­ern con­ve­niences and retail goods of all kinds at unheard of prices. Begin­ning in 1908, Sears start­ed sell­ing entire hous­es, in approx­i­mate­ly 25-ton kits trans­port­ed by rail­road, con­sist­ing of 30,000 pre-cut parts, plumb­ing and elec­tri­cal fix­tures, and up to 750 pounds of nails.
“In an era before com­mer­cial avi­a­tion and long-haul truck­ing,” Curbed mar­vels, “Sears, Roe­buck & Co. set up an oper­a­tion that would pack­age and ship more than 400 dif­fer­ent types of homes and build­ings to any­body who had the cash and access to a cat­a­log.”
They start­ed small, and just as they didn’t come up with the con­cept of the mail order cat­a­log, Sears didn’t invent the kit house, though they sug­gest as much in their telling of the sto­ry. Instead they may have tak­en the idea from anoth­er com­pa­ny called Aladdin. Aladdin hous­es have been for­got­ten, how­ev­er, and even Sears’ main com­peti­tor, Mont­gomery Ward, didn’t catch up until 1921 and only last­ed ten years in the kit house busi­ness.

Sears hous­es, on the oth­er hand, are cel­e­brat­ed and sought out as mod­els of the ear­ly 20th cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can home, and for good rea­son. Between 1908 and 1939, Sears sold 70–75,000 hous­es in 447 dif­fer­ent styles all over the coun­try. “From Crafts­man to Cape Cods, they offered a cus­tom home at bud­gets and sizes that could accom­mo­date any size fam­i­ly,” writes Pop­u­lar Mechan­ics.
These Sears homes weren’t cheap low-end hous­es. Many of them were built using the finest qual­i­ty build­ing mate­ri­als avail­able dur­ing that time. It’s not uncom­mon to find Sears homes today with oak floors, cypress sid­ing, and cedar shin­gles.
What’s even more extra­or­di­nary is that 50% of these were built by the home­own­ers them­selves, usu­al­ly, as in a barn-rais­ing, with the gen­er­ous help of fam­i­ly, friends, and neigh­bors. The oth­er half sold were built pro­fes­sion­al­ly. “Often,” writes Messy Nessy, “local builders and car­pen­try com­pa­nies pur­chased homes from Sears to build as mod­el homes and mar­ket their ser­vices to poten­tial cus­tomers.”
These hous­es could have a sig­nif­i­cant effect on the char­ac­ter of a neigh­bor­hood. Not only could poten­tial buy­ers see first­hand, and par­tic­i­pate in, the con­struc­tion. They could also order the same or a sim­i­lar mod­el, cus­tomize it, and even—as the com­pa­ny tells us in its own short his­to­ry of the “Sears Mod­ern Home”—design their own homes and “sub­mit the blue­prints to Sears, which would then ship off the appro­pri­ate pre­cut and fit­ted mate­ri­als.”

Sears sounds mod­est about its impact. The com­pa­ny writes it was not “an inno­v­a­tive home design­er” but instead “a very able fol­low­er of pop­u­lar home designs but with the added advan­tage of mod­i­fy­ing hous­es and hard­ware accord­ing to buy­er tastes.” Yet Sears hous­es aren’t beloved for their for­ward-look­ing designs, but for their stur­di­ness and vari­ety, as well as for their impact on “the emo­tion­al lives of rur­al folk,” as Messy Nessy puts it.
“The Sears mail-order cat­a­logues were sit­ting on kitchen coun­ter­tops inside mil­lions of Amer­i­can homes, allow­ing poten­tial home­own­ers to both visu­al­ize their new home and pur­chase it as eas­i­ly as they might have bought a new toast­er.” Build­ing a house required a lit­tle more invest­ment than plug­ging in a toast­er, and required a 75-page instruc­tion book, but that’s anoth­er part of why Sears house hunters are such a ded­i­cat­ed bunch, awestruck at each still-stand­ing mod­el they’re able to pho­to­graph and match up with its cat­a­log illus­tra­tions and floor plans.
In its first year of pro­duc­tion, 1908, Sears sold only one mod­el, num­ber 125, an Eight-Room Bun­ga­low Style House for $945, adver­tised as “the finest cot­tage ever con­struct­ed at a price less than $1500.” In 1918, the com­pa­ny moved from a num­ber­ing sys­tem to named mod­els, most of which sound like the names of cozy small towns and bed­room com­mu­ni­ties: Ade­line, Bel­mont, Maple­wood, Aval­on, Kil­bourne, Del Ray, Stone Ridge…. (See a full list of these mod­els at The Arts & Crafts Soci­ety web­site.)

In the years Sears sold hous­es, between 54 and 44 per­cent of Amer­i­cans lived in rur­al areas, and these con­sti­tut­ed Sears’ most loy­al cus­tomers, giv­en that the cat­a­log allowed them to pur­chase things they could buy nowhere else, includ­ing ten room colo­nial man­sions like The Mag­no­lia, avail­able from 1913 to 1922 for $6,488, or rough­ly $88,000—a steal if you can put in the work. This was the largest and most expen­sive mod­el the com­pa­ny offered, “a three-sto­ry, eight room neo-Geor­gian with a two-sto­ry columned por­ti­co, porte-cochere, and sleep­ing porch­es.” (Mint juleps and ser­vants’ quar­ters not includ­ed.)
Sears even­tu­al­ly offered three build qual­i­ties, Hon­or Bilt, Stan­dard Built, and Sim­plex Sec­tion­al. At the low­est end of the price and build spec­trum, the com­pa­ny notes, “Sim­plex hous­es were fre­quent­ly only a cou­ple of rooms and were ide­al for sum­mer cot­tages.” Many of its low-end and ear­ly mod­els did not include bath­rooms, and the com­pa­ny sold out­hous­es sep­a­rate­ly. But due to inno­v­a­tive con­struc­tion meth­ods, even the least expen­sive hous­es held up well.
Because the com­pa­ny lost most of the records after its kit house busi­ness fold­ed, it can be dif­fi­cult to iden­ti­fy a Sears house. And because even the “youngest of Sears homes,” Pop­u­lar Mechan­ics points out, is now going on nine decades old, they all require a sig­nif­i­cant amount of care.” The blog Kit House Hunters has found over 18,000 Sears hous­es still stand­ing across the coun­try, most of them in the North­east and Mid­west, where they sold best. (One com­mu­ni­ty in Elgin, IL has over 200 ver­i­fied Sears homes.)


	

In the video at the top, you can see a few of those well-built Sears hous­es still lived in today. The short How to Archi­tect video above points out that “Sears had a mas­sive impact on the busi­ness of home-build­ing, and… the busi­ness of pre-fab­ri­ca­tion, is alive and well today.” For a look at the vari­ety and intri­ca­cy of the Sears Mod­ern Home designs, see this Flickr gallery with over 80 images of cat­a­log pages, illus­trat­ed homes, and floor plans. And if you think you might be liv­ing in one of these hous­es, many of which have been grant­ed his­toric sta­tus, find out with this handy 9‑step guide for iden­ti­fy­ing a Sears Kit Home.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

title: 'The Department of Objects' Brings the Charm of Sleep-Away Camp to Chicago
description: For the last decade, our good friend and collaborator Jeroen Smeets of The Jaunt, has facilitated journeys for artists to some of the most far-flu
body:
For the last decade, our good friend and collaborator Jeroen Smeets of The Jaunt, has facilitated journeys for artists to some of the most far-flung places on Earth as part of week-long residencies in destinations of their choosing. Building on the limitless inspiration of travel and seeking to grow The Jaunt community, Smeets first hosted a Winter Camp in 2024 that invited four artists to spend time together in close quarters, hemmed in by winter weather and providing a welcome respite for the cross pollination of ideas, art, food, stories, and adventures.
For the third iteration of Winter Camp, Joy Machine and The Jaunt teamed up to bring four artists from balmy California to the frigid tundra of the Midwest, subjecting them to a proper winter for the first time in their lives with frozen lakes, sledding, snowballs, and temperatures reaching a sublime 4 degrees Fahrenheit. The destination? The historic and picturesque Camp Wandawega, located just a short trek north of Chicago in Elkhorn, Wisconsin.
Wyatt Hersey, “View from Wandawega Lodge” (2026), gouache on birch panel, 20 x 20 inches
Wyatt Hersey, Melissa Lakey, Esther Pearl Watson, and Anna Valdez joined us in the lodges, kitchens, and bunk houses of Camp Wandawega for five days of arctic magic and only superficial frostbite. The grounds of Camp Wandawega date back more than 100 years and first served as a speakeasy and brothel during Prohibition, before being converted to a summer camp by the Latvian Catholic church. Nowadays, it operates as a truly unique retreat with all the hallmarks of a traditional sleepaway camp, a place that exudes Americana and hearkens to endless days of communion and play that feel so sorely lacking in our digital age. Encased in February ice, we explored every frosted meadow and outbuilding of the camp on daily hikes, wrapped in layers of nostalgia. Did we mention it was also cold?
At camp, the artists were immediately drawn to a cozy attic storage room called the Department of Objects, quickly dubbed The Green Room (or “the warmest space we can reasonably be expected to work”), which is an extraordinary lending library of old magazines, vintage fishing lures, plaid everything, dusty books, patches, and all matter of camp ephemera from generations past–some of which joins us in the gallery. A genuine treasure trove of inspiration and this exhibition’s namesake, the Department of Objects provided countless of hours of painting and drawing that manifested in the work you see here.
You can RSVP to the opening reception of The Department of Objects from 6 to 8 p.m. on October 23 or sign up for the collector preview. All four artists will be present! 
Anna Valdez, “Assorted Vintage Lures” (2026), 12 x 10 inches
Melissa Lakey, “Vintage Radios” (2026), acrylic on wood panel, 11 x 14 inches
The Department of Objects at Camp Wandawega, Elkhorn, Wisconsin

title: A New Wildlife Crossing in Colorado Has Already Cut Vehicle Collisions by 91 Percent
description: Anyone who has driven Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs knows that traffic can get… hairy. And it’s not just drivers whose safety
body:
Anyone who has driven Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs knows that traffic can get… hairy. And it’s not just drivers whose safety is at risk, as animals like elk, bears, coyotes, and more also need to use the highway to access 39,000 acres of habitat. Cars and pronghorns just aren’t compatible. That’s why Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT) set out to build a wildlife-only bridge, the largest of its kind currently in North America, which it completed in December 2025. Within the first nine months since its opening, wildlife-vehicle collisions were already down a whopping 91 percent.
Before the crossing opened, dozens of animals were killed by vehicles every year, often up to one per day during migration seasons. The overpass spans I-25’s six lanes and is completely covered in grass so that critters have uninterrupted access to habitat on both sides of the highway—and drivers face less risk and expense due to collisions. The project is one of several in progress across the U.S., including a handful more in Colorado that include underpasses and smaller bridges. Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist with Colorado Parks and Wildlife, told CBS News, “One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when CDOT sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under I-25.”

title: Álvaro Urbano Honors the Lost Specimens of Mexico City's Iconic Casa Cueva
description: Nested in a natural lava cave in Mexico City’s Pedregal de San Ángel region, a sprawling, mosaic-laden domicile was once home to Juan and Helen Fo
body:
Nested in a natural lava cave in Mexico City’s Pedregal de San Ángel region, a sprawling, mosaic-laden domicile was once home to Juan and Helen Fowler O’Gorman, an architect and artist, respectively. The pair designed the icon of modernist Mexican architecture, called Casa Cueva, in 1954, although it was largely destroyed after the couple sold the home in 1969.
At Museo Jumex, Álvaro Urbano presents an homage to the innovations of Casa Cueva, drawing on its gardens and the legacy that Helen left behind, particularly through her 1961 book titled Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants. Written and illustrated while she lived at Casa Cueva, the rich volume documented a variety of the region’s native specimens. For Urbano, these vegetal renderings became the basis of a new body of metal sculptures.
Installation view of ‘Álvaro Urbano: Helen’ at Museo Jumex (2026). Photo byRamiro Chávez
The artist’s solo exhibition, Helen, suspends his signature painted plants in a delicate arrangement. Floating against a diaphanous curtain, the lifelike sculptures appear almost as apparitions, hovering in mid-air to guide viewers through the dreamy space.
Each specimen is based off of one that appeared in Helen’s book, and a site-specific installation reveals variegated stone amid a floor of square pavers. Like Casa Cueva, the exhibition unfolds organically, creating a continual dialogue between space, plants, and those able to witness both.
Helen is on view through February 7. Explore more of Urbano’s work on Instagram

title: Dozens of Sculptures Dot Bondi Beach in the 2026 Sculpture by the Sea Exhibition
description: Bondi Beach, a neighborhood east of central Sydney, is about as iconic a surf spot as they come. Its eponymous crescent beach glows with golden sa
body:
Bondi Beach, a neighborhood east of central Sydney, is about as iconic a surf spot as they come. Its eponymous crescent beach glows with golden sand, and its cliffs frame stunning scenery. In December 2025, it was also the site of a tragic terrorist attack, when two men opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration, killing 15 people. (Gun deaths, let alone mass shootings, are exceedingly rare in Australia, especially compared to the U.S.) At Bondi, heroism and a sense of community converged in its beautiful setting, reinforcing pride of place. And it’s again home, at least temporarily, to “the world’s largest free to the public sculpture exhibition.”
Sculpture by the Sea organizes an annual outdoor presentation of dozens of sculptures every year along a 1.25-mile stretch of coastline, highlighting work by artists from around the world. Styles and materials vary greatly, from geometric abstraction to myriad representational forms. Emma Anna’s “DREAM_N” resembles a giant Scrabble letter rack, while Andre Braun’s “Surface Breach” depicts a giant hand breaking free from the earth.
Emma Anna (Colombia-NSW), “DREAM_N” (2026)
The show remains on view through November 2. Explore past editions and watch a video of sculptures from last year’s exhibition below. See more on Instagram.
